sections.description: Introduces the patient’s demographic profile, presenting symptoms, relevant family history, physical examination findings, and the first set of laboratory investigations that prompted consideration of an atypical form of diabetes.
subtopics: Age 22 male with hyperglycaemia detected during routine health check
Symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, recent weight loss
Family pedigree showing three generations with early‐onset diabetes (maternal grandmother, mother, brother)
Physical exam: BMI 24.6 kg/m², blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, absence of acanthosis nigricans
Initial laboratory panel:
- Fasting plasma glucose 12.4 mmol/L
- HbA1c 10.2 % (88 mmol/mol)
- OGTT 75 g → 19.8 mmol/L at 2 h
- Lipid profile revealing triglycerides 4.31 mmol/L and HDL 1.01 mmol/L
- No ketoacidosis
- Negative pancreatic autoantibodies (GADA, IA‑2A)
- Glucagon stimulation test C‑peptide 0.39→0.83 nmol/L

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis – Distinguishing MODY from Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes
sections.description: Systematic evaluation of the clinical picture using laboratory data and validated tools to separate monogenic diabetes from autoimmune or insulin‑resistant forms.
subtopics: Core features distinguishing type 1 diabetes:
- Presence of islet autoantibodies
- Rapid loss of C‑peptide
- Typically lean phenotype
Core features distinguishing type 2 diabetes:
- Evidence of insulin resistance (obesity/acanthosis nigricans)
- Dyslipidaemia pattern consistent with metabolic syndrome
- Often preserved C‑peptide early on
Interpretation of patient data:
- Negative GADA/IA‑2A argues against autoimmune diabetes
- Stimulated C‑peptide 0.83 nmol/L indicates limited but present β‑cell reserve
- BMI near overweight yet no acanthosis nigricans reduces likelihood of classic T2DM
- Marked postprandial hyperglycaemia suggests β‑cell secretory defect rather than resistance
Application of the Exeter MODY probability calculator:
- Estimated probability ≈62 % based on entered variables
- Discussion of limitations when applied to non‑European ancestry populations
Rationale for maintaining MODY suspicion despite overlapping features

sections.section_title: Genetic Testing & Molecular Pathogenesis in HNF1A-MODY
sections.description: Details the indication for molecular diagnostics, technical aspects of next‑generation sequencing panels, variant classification according to ACMG guidelines, and functional consequences of loss‑of‑function mutations in the HNF1A gene.
subtopics: Indication for genetic workup after high clinical suspicion
NGS‐based targeted MODY panel:
- Coverage includes >15 known MODY genes
- Workflow from DNA extraction to bioinformatic variant calling
- Turnaround time compatible with urgent clinical decision making
ACMG criteria applied to the identified variant:
- Variant nomenclature: c.809A>G (p.Asn270Ser) in exon 4
- Classified as pathogenic/likely pathogenic based on:
-- Absence from population databases (gnomAD) and ClinVar/VarSome
-- In silico pathogenicity score AlphaMissense 0.995
-- Localization within DNA‑binding domain adjacent to known pathogenic residues
-- Co‐segregation with diabetes in three affected relatives
-- De novo or inherited autosomal dominant pattern inferred from pedigree
Functional impact of HNF1A loss:
- Transcription factor regulating INS gene expression & GLUT2 transporter in β‐cells → reduced glucose sensing/secretion
- Regulation of hepatic gluconeogenic enzymes → modest effect on fasting glucose
- Transcriptional control over renal SGLT2 → lowered renal glucose threshold resulting in glycosuria
- Progressive decline in β‐cell mass explaining worsening hyperglycaemia over years

sections.description: Explains how the confirmed HNF1A mutation reshaped pharmacologic management—from an empiric insulin‐based regimen to a precision-medicine approach employing agents that exploit residual β‐cell function while minimizing hypoglycaemia risk.
subtopics: Initial empiric regimen prior to genetic results:
- Basal insulin degludec (8 U daily) + metformin 1500 mg + saxagliptin 5 mg
- Rationale: rapid control assuming T2DM phenotype with possible insulin resistance
"Transition after genetic confirmation":
- Discontinuation of basal insulin once HbA1c fell below 9 % and residual C‑peptide evident
- Initiation of dulaglutide weekly (GLP‑1 receptor agonist) while continuing metformin
* Benefits specific to HNF1A-MODY:
-- Enhances glucose‐dependent insulin secretion without overstimulating K_ATP channels
-- Lower hypoglycaemia risk compared with sulfonylureas when β‐cell reserve wanes
-- Promotes weight loss beneficial in borderline overweight patients
-- Improves postprandial glucose excursions characteristic of this genotype
-- Potential cardiovascular benefit consistent with GLP‑1 RA class effects
* Alternative first-line option discussed: low-dose sulfonylureas (e.g., glimepiride)
-- Evidence that sulfonylureas achieve glycaemic control rapidly in HNF1A-MODY
-- Higher hypoglycaemia risk when β‐cell function declines
* Why SGLT2 inhibitors were avoided:
-- Underlying reduced SGLT2 expression predisposes to marked glucosuria
-- Heightened risk for volume depletion and euglycaemic ketoacidosis
-- Lack of robust benefit data in this monogenic subset
* Role of continued DPP‑4 inhibition:
-- May provide modest additive incretin effect without increasing hypoglycaemia
-- Retained while patient stable on metformin/dulaglutide combo
